Pilgrimage

/PIL-grim-ij/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Pilgrimage means a long, purposeful journey undertaken for a deeply meaningful goal, often spiritual.

Pilgrimage means a long, purposeful journey undertaken for a deeply meaningful goal, often spiritual. Every spring, thousands make the pilgrimage on foot to the shrine at the mountain's summit.

Worked Example

Sixty years after the war separated them, the two sisters learned each other's addresses at last. The elder was eighty-four and hated airports, buses, and boats equally. She took all three anyway — eleven days of travel across two oceans, carrying their mother's ring the whole way. Friends called the trip too hard at her age; she called it the one journey her life had been waiting for. It was not a vacation. It was a pilgrimage.

The journey's great length and hardship, endured for one deeply meaningful purpose — reunion and the carrying of the mother's ring — is what makes it a pilgrimage rather than a trip.

How Pilgrimage Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

quest

quest: a journey in search of something important

Antonyms

stroll

stroll: a short, casual walk

wandering

wandering: aimless movement

How Strong Is It? — trip → pilgrimage → odyssey

trip vs. pilgrimage

trip vs. pilgrimage: Trip is the weak, everyday word — any travel counts; a pilgrimage adds distance, effort, and above all a deeply meaningful purpose.

odyssey vs. pilgrimage

odyssey vs. pilgrimage: Odyssey is stronger in scale than pilgrimage — years of wandering and ordeal — though a pilgrimage keeps the sharper sense of one sacred destination.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — pilgrim

Root — pilgrim: wanderer, foreigner (Latin peregrinus, 'through the fields')

Suffix — -age

Suffix — -age: noun-forming: act or result of

Put it together

Put it together: Pilgrimage traces to Latin peregrinus, 'foreigner, wanderer' — literally per agros, 'through the fields,' describing someone traveling beyond their own land. Old French wore the word down to pelegrin, English to pilgrim, and -age made the journey itself a noun. The unshrunken Latin survives in peregrine, the falcon named for its vast wanderings.

Use the root in a new word: peregrine

Use the root in a new word: peregrine: The peregrine falcon crosses whole continents on migration — peregrine literally means 'wanderer from abroad,' the same Latin peregrinus that shrank over centuries into the word pilgrim.
